newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Brazil to adjust, not reform, pensions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brazil to adjust, not reform, pensions.

text.p: Brazil's long-awaited pension reform bill represents little more than a tinkering of its bankrupt social security system, Social Security Minister Reinhold Stephanes said.

But a rewrite of the bill currently taking place in the Senate should be enough to keep a check on deficits over the next ten years during which time deeper reforms could take place, Stephanes told Reuters.
"It's more of an adjustment than a reform," the minister said in an interview.
The government wants to make the social security system viable by linking pensions to contributions, and not to time served as currently, and by scrapping civil servants' perks.
But last year an original draft of the pension reform bill was dealt a shock defeat by the Chamber of Deputies and a revised version only passed after being stripped of its most important points.

Then, as the government turned all its attention to a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election next year, pension reform, along with a shake-up of the civil service, was put on the backburner.
Re-election has now been approved in the Chamber of Deputies and the government, seeking to revive its reform program, has appointed a senator to rewrite the pension reform bill.
Stephanes said the new-look legislation would be meaningless if the following points were not included:
-- minimum retirement ages of 60 for men and 55 for women, rising over ten years to 65 and 60 respectively;
-- an end to partial pensions paid to workers after set periods of time served and who may continue to work;
-- an end to automatic raises in the value of pensions to match increases awarded to salary-earners;

"These changes (including the linking of pensions to contributions) would give us a 10-year horizon of relative calm during which time it would be possible to implement deeper reforms," Stephanes said.

The minister said a bill creating tax incentives for private pension plan holders would be sent to Congress once the pension reform bill was approved. About one million Brazilians have private pension plans while 16 million are on state pensions.

Brazil's social security system went into the red last year with a $500 million deficit expected to rise to bewteen $1.5-2.0 billion in 1997 and $3.0 billion in 1998. The deficit would reach $30 billion by the year 2030, equivalent to 4.2 percent of GDP, if nothing was done to reform the system.
Stephanes said the mininum age requirement would provide immediate relief for the system by reducing the number of people seeking retirement to about 600,000 a year from 800,000 now.

And by scrapping a wide range of pension perks for civil servants, the government hopes to ease the payroll burden for endebted state and municipal governments. Last year, Espirito Santo state's personnel costs were the equivalent of 110 percent of receipts. In mighty Sao Paulo, the figure was 89 percent.
"Really the situation could not get any worse in the public sector," Stephanes said. "In the private sector, it's the outlook that's grave."
The federal government lavished about $17 billion on pensions for just 873,000 civil servants in 1996, compared with $40 billion on 16.6 million pensioners from the private sector.

But as Brazil's population continues to age, so demand for private pensions will rise. The number of people over 65 is set to rise to 7.7 percent of the total population by 2020, up from an estimated 5.1 percent in 2000 and 3.1 percent in 1970.

The government is also concerned Brazil might become a social security haven within the four-nation Mercosur customs union and wants to bring its system into line with the leaner pension laws of its neighbors.
"There will be a very mobile workforce in Mercosur and we need to have matching systems," Stephanes said.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 5561 2230358))
